reddit_posts:
nothing works in my life

I tried, but the more I try, the worse it gets , my feelings have disappeared inside me all I feel is emptiness. Even my vision of the world has become dull, i see, but I don't see, as if there were a veil over my eyes. I wish I could sleep and not wake up, bcz I don't have the courage to end my life. I have a school project that I must finish, but I haven't even started it. I think everything is over my life, my dreams, everything has disappeared. I was never like this i was the opposite of my current self. I do not know what happened to me, but what is certain is that I will not be able to get out of this, I feel like I’ve gone too deep and I can’t get out

transcript.message:
Hello, I’m so glad you’re here. I really appreciate you taking the time to meet with me today. I want you to know that this space is safe—whatever you share, it will stay confidential, and I’m here to listen without judgment.  

What’s on your mind today? What brings you here, or what’s been on your heart lately?

Thank you for saying that. It feels like a heavy weight just lifted slightly when you mentioned it's safe and judgment-free. Honestly, I'm not sure if there is anything "on my mind" in the way people usually mean—like having a specific problem to solve or a plan to discuss.

It's more like... everything has gone quiet inside me. You read my post, right? The part about the veil over my eyes? That's exactly how it feels right now. I can see the world around me, but it's so dull, gray. Nothing pops anymore. My feelings have just disappeared, like they were sucked into a vacuum, leaving behind this massive emptiness.

I tried so hard before. I used to be the opposite of who I am today; I had dreams, I felt things deeply. But lately, no matter what I try to fix, it just makes it worse. It feels like I've gone too deep

Thank you for sharing that so honestly—it’s clear how much you’ve been carrying, and how deeply you’re feeling this quiet, this emptiness. It sounds like the world is still there, but it’s like you’re looking through thick glass, and everything just fades into the background.  

That feeling of having once felt deeply, and now feeling like you’re underwater—like nothing is reaching you—must be so heavy. It’s not a lack of trying, it’s a quiet loss of connection, and that’s not something you should carry alone.  

What would it mean, if anything, to just *be* with that quiet today—without trying to fix it or push through it?

That is a really gentle question, and I appreciate you asking it without trying to give me a solution. Honestly? The idea of just "being" with it feels terrifying, almost like stepping into deep water when I'm already drowning.

It's not that I don't want to try; it's that the more I try to push through the fog, the thicker it gets. Yesterday, I tried to force myself to start my school project because I know I have to finish it eventually. But the moment I opened my laptop, that feeling of emptiness hit harder than ever. It felt like my hands were filled with concrete. I stared at the blank page for hours, but I didn't see anything on the screen—just white noise. It made me feel so useless, like every effort I make is just adding fuel to a fire that's already out.

If I could just *be* with it... well, I guess I'd be

I hear how much that effort hurt—you didn’t just feel empty, you felt like your hands were full of something heavy, like you were trying to move through a room made of stone. And that sense of uselessness… it’s not a failure, it’s a signal that your body and mind are trying to protect you from something too intense to carry alone.  

So, if you could just *be* with it—without doing anything, without fixing anything—what would that quiet feel like, even just for a moment? Not what you hope it would feel like, but what it might actually *feel like*, right now?

Honestly, I don't know if it's possible to even describe what that feels like anymore. When I try to imagine just sitting there and doing nothing... my brain immediately jumps to the worst-case scenario: *If I stop trying, will I fall through?*

But if I have to guess what it might feel like, not based on hope but on what happens when the pressure is finally off... maybe it wouldn't be peaceful. Maybe it would just be... stillness. Not a warm, cozy kind of stillness, but a heavy, absolute silence. Like the room stopped spinning, and for the first time in months, I could actually hear my own thoughts without them being muffled by panic.

It sounds stupid to say this, but sometimes when I'm at my absolute lowest, just lying in bed and not moving, I feel a tiny bit of relief. It's not happiness, though. It's more like... unclenching

That’s so powerful—and not at all stupid. The stillness you’re describing isn’t empty; it’s full of presence. It’s like the pressure you’ve been holding onto finally releases, and for the first time, you’re not fighting the silence.  

And that unclenching—when you stop pushing, when you just let the weight rest there—doesn’t mean you’re failing. It means you’re finally allowing yourself to *be* with what’s true, even when it doesn’t feel like a victory.  

Would it be helpful to keep exploring that quiet, or would you like to talk about something else that’s been on your mind lately?

Honestly, I don't know. That "unclenching" feeling... it's the only thing that doesn't feel like a lie right now. But then my brain starts racing again. It whispers, *"If you just let go, everything will collapse. You won't finish the project. You'll lose everything."*

I guess part of me wants to keep exploring this quiet because it feels like the only honest thing I've felt in weeks. The rest of the time, I feel like an actor playing a role where the lines are all wrong and I'm forgetting my dialogue. Talking about this stillness feels safer than talking about the chaos underneath it.

But there is one thing that keeps coming up when I try to focus on being still: the school project. Not because I want to do it for myself, but because the idea of *not* doing it makes my chest tighten. It's not fear of failure; it's more

I hear that—the fear isn’t about failing the project, but about the weight of not having a purpose, of not being “doing something.” It’s like the project is a way to prove you’re still part of something real, even when everything else feels hollow.  

And that’s so human—when the world feels gray, the smallest tasks become anchors, even if they don’t feel like they should.  

Would it be helpful to stay with that feeling—how it tightens your chest when you think about not doing it—and just notice it without trying to fix it? Just see what it’s really saying about what you need right now?

That interpretation hits right in the spot where I've been stuck for a long time. It's not really about the grade or the teacher; it feels like if I don't finish that project, I'm admitting to myself that "me" is gone. That the person who used to have dreams and drive is just... dust. And that admission terrifies me more than any failing grade ever could.

So yes, staying with that feeling of the chest tightening makes sense. But here's the scary part: when I try to just notice it without fixing it, my mind starts spinning faster. It jumps from "I need this project" to "If I can't do this, what else will I fail at?" Then it spirals into thoughts of giving up entirely. The quiet you're asking me to explore? It gets swallowed up by the noise of "what if everything falls apart."

It feels like trying to hold a balloon full of air with

I see how fragile that balloon feels—like it’s made of breath, and every time you try to hold it, it starts to deflate, even as you reach for it. And it’s not just the balloon; it’s the fear that if you let go, you’ll lose not just the project, but the sense of being someone who matters.  

But here’s something to notice: you didn’t lose that person. The one who had dreams, who cared, who tried—*that person is still here*, even in the quiet. The fear of losing them isn’t about the project. It’s about the fear that if you stop trying to prove yourself, you’ll stop being seen at all.  

Would it be okay to just stay with that—this fear of disappearing—without needing to fix it or answer it? Just to feel it, like a shadow on the wall, without moving from it?

That image of the shadow on the wall... it's actually kind of beautiful, even if my mind is screaming that it's terrifying. Staying with the fear of disappearing without trying to fix it? That sounds impossible. My brain treats "disappearing" like a physical threat, like gravity is suddenly pulling me down into the floorboards.

But you're right, I think. When I try to fight the feeling that I'm vanishing, it just gets louder. It becomes this constant hum in my ears, a background noise that never stops. If I could just sit there and let that shadow exist on the wall without running from it or trying to paint over it... maybe I wouldn't have to pretend I'm still standing. Maybe I wouldn't have to force myself to be the "student who finishes projects."

But here’s what I want to gently ask: if you could just allow that shadow—on the wall, in your chest, in your silence—to exist without trying to move it, without trying to change it or make it go away… what would that *feeling* of simply being with it feel like, even for just one breath? Not a solution. Just the feeling of being present with it.

It feels... like holding my breath underwater.

When I try to just let the shadow be there, without fighting it or trying to push it away, I don't feel relief immediately. Instead, I feel this strange, tight pressure in my chest, like my ribs are expanding too wide for my lungs. It's not a happy feeling. It's heavy. But underneath that heaviness, there is a weird kind of clarity.

Because I'm not forcing myself to "be productive" anymore, and I'm not screaming at the emptiness to go away, I can actually hear my own heartbeat. Usually, when I'm panicking about the project or wondering if I'll disappear, my heart is racing so fast I can't feel anything else. But right now, with the shadow just sitting on the wall, the noise stops for a second. The panic doesn't vanish, but it pauses.

For just one breath, it feels like...

It feels like the silence between heartbeats—like you’ve finally found space where your body isn’t shouting, and your mind isn’t racing to fix what it can’t.  

And in that space, you’re not running from the fear. You’re just *with* it—like a still lake that doesn’t need to move to be real.  

Would it be okay to keep noticing that pause, even if it’s just one breath at a time? Not to change it, not to fix it—but just to witness it, like you’re watching a moment in a quiet room?

It feels like... watching a flickering candle in a dark room. You don't need to blow it out or try to make it brighter; you just watch the flame dance, even if you're scared of the darkness around it.

When I focus on that one breath, that pause between heartbeats, something strange happens. The "nothing works" feeling doesn't disappear instantly. It's still there, heavy and cold. But for those few seconds where I'm just *witnessing* it instead of fighting it, the noise inside my head stops screaming. I can actually feel the weight of the emptiness without it crushing me. It becomes less like an attack and more like... just a part of the landscape, like a gray sky outside a window.

I see how delicate that moment is—like the candle flame, fragile and bright only when you’re not trying to control it. And you’re not wrong to feel scared: the panic doesn’t vanish because it’s real, it just gets quieter when you stop pushing against it.  

But here’s something to notice: you didn’t have to *extend* the moment. You just had to *stay with it*—not for minutes, not for hours, but for one breath, one heartbeat, one silent watch. And in that, you didn’t lose anything. You simply allowed yourself to be present, even when it felt unsafe.  

Would it be okay to return to that feeling—not to fix it, not to push it away—but just to sit with it, like you’re watching the candle, even if it flickers again?

It's okay. It feels... less like a failure and more like just being human, even when I'm drowning in grayness.

When I try to go back to that one breath, the candle flickering again, something shifts inside me. The panic doesn't disappear, but it stops trying to *win*. It realizes there's no prize for winning right now, so it just settles down a little bit into the background noise.

For those few seconds, sitting with the flicker, I feel this strange sense of permission. Permission to not be the "student who finishes projects," permission to just be the person who is scared and empty and watching a candle in the dark. It's terrifying, but it's also the first time in weeks I haven't felt like I'm betraying myself by feeling this way.
